articles.title: The wasps that horrified Darwin reveal evolution's one-way streets
articles.dek: Few insects have a more gruesome lifestyle than Darwin wasps.
paragraphs: Few insects have a more gruesome lifestyle than Darwin wasps. Rather than simply hunting other animals, these parasitic wasps lay their eggs on or inside living hosts, including caterpillars, beetles and spiders. Their larvae then feed on their hosts, gradually consuming them and eventually killing them.

This disturbing biology fascinated Charles Darwin. In an 1860 letter to American botanist Asa Gray, he questioned how a benevolent God could have deliberately created creatures that feed "within the living bodies of caterpillars." This famous observation later inspired the name Darwin wasps for the insect family Ichneumonidae, which includes more than 25,000 described species.

Different species employ remarkably different strategies. Some wasps permanently paralyze their hosts before laying their eggs, effectively turning them into immobile food supplies for their offspring. Others adopt a more intricate approach: they allow their hosts to remain alive, feeding and growing even as the developing wasp larvae consume them.

These contrasting strategies offer a window into a fundamental question in evolutionary biology: how predictable is evolution? Scientists have long recognized that similar adaptations can arise independently in different organisms, suggesting that evolution sometimes arrives at the same solutions again and again. But a related question has received less attention: when evolution takes a particular direction, how easily can it turn back?

Now, an international team of scientists led by the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin has used Darwin wasps to investigate this question, revealing that some evolutionary innovations arise repeatedly but are almost never reversed.

By analyzing genetic data from 697 wasp species, representing every major lineage of Darwin wasps, researchers reconstructed the evolutionary history of these strategies. They discovered a striking pattern: the transition from paralyzing hosts to allowing them to continue developing occurred independently at least 23 times, but they found no evidence of reversals. Similarly, the evolution of larvae developing inside rather than outside their hosts occurred repeatedly but was only rarely reversed.

"Evolution doesn't necessarily keep all its options open," explains Bernardo F. Santos, lead author of the study and researcher at the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin. "Once a wasp lineage evolves a close relationship with a living, developing host, returning to its ancestral strategy seems extremely difficult. It's something like an evolutionary ratchet: you can move forward, but going backward becomes nearly impossible."

The study, published in the journal Current Biology , provides compelling evidence that evolution can be both remarkably repeatable and strongly directional. Different lineages independently arrived at similar solutions, yet almost never returned to their previous ways of life.

The findings highlight how evolution is shaped not only by chance and natural selection, but also by the constraints imposed by an organism's own evolutionary history. Rather than an unlimited exploration of possibilities, evolution may follow paths that become increasingly difficult to abandon once taken.

articles.title: Air holes turn silicon wafers into flat ultraviolet focusing mirrors for compact optics
articles.dek: Traditional lenses and mirrors focus light using curved surfaces.
paragraphs: Traditional lenses and mirrors focus light using curved surfaces. Metasurfaces can achieve similar functions with a flat layer of nanoscale structures that locally control the phase of light. Extending these flat optics into the ultraviolet could support compact systems for high-resolution imaging, spectroscopy, and sensing, but it introduces a fundamental materials problem: many of the materials used to make metasurfaces strongly absorb UV light.

Researchers at the University of Stuttgart have developed an alternative approach that turns this limitation on its head. Rather than trying to make an absorbing material transparent, their metasurface confines much of the light inside tiny air-filled cavities etched directly into silicon.

The device focuses reflected ultraviolet light at a wavelength of 325 nm and demonstrates a new approach to controlling light in wavelength ranges where suitable transparent materials can be difficult to find.
The research is published in the journal Advanced Photonics .

Many conventional dielectric metasurfaces rely on tiny pillars made from materials with a high refractive index. Light becomes concentrated inside the pillars, and variations in their geometry allow the metasurface to control the emerging wavefront. Silicon works well for this purpose at visible and longer wavelengths, but becomes strongly absorbing in the ultraviolet. Light confined within a silicon resonator would therefore be lost rather than efficiently redirected.

Structures called Mie voids invert this concept. Instead of forming resonators from solid pillars surrounded by air, the researchers etched small air cavities into bulk silicon. Light entering a void reflects from the surrounding silicon boundaries, creating a resonant mode concentrated predominantly in the air cavity, where absorption is negligible. This reduces the optical field's overlap with the absorbing silicon.

Counterintuitively, silicon's strong absorption at ultraviolet wavelengths can contribute to this confinement. The complex optical properties that accompany absorption increase the reflectivity of the air-silicon interface, helping light remain confined within the void. The strategy therefore does not eliminate silicon's UV absorption. Instead, it uses the optical properties of the absorbing material while keeping much of the resonant field away from it.

To turn these resonators into a focusing element, the voids are shaped as ellipses approximately 470 nanometers long and 100 nanometers deep. When circularly polarized light illuminates an elliptical void, the reflected light acquires a so-called geometric phase equal to twice the void's rotation angle. By varying this rotation across the half-millimeter-sized metasurface, a focusing profile is encoded directly into the silicon. Under a standard optical microscope, this arrangement appears as colored ring patterns, making the encoded focusing design directly visible.

When illuminated at an incidence angle of 45 degrees with 325 nanometer UV light, these metasurfaces act as flat equivalents of off-axis parabolic mirrors, redirecting the beam by 90 degrees while focusing it. Metasurfaces with focal lengths from 5 millimeters down to 1. 25 millimeters were fabricated and produced circular focal spots as small as about 1 micrometer. Up to a numerical aperture of 0. 15, the spots approached the diffraction limit, which is the fundamental resolution bound set by the wave nature of light.

The versatility of possible wavefront shaping is further demonstrated by adding a spiral phase to the layout, generating so-called orbital angular momentum beams. They can be understood as light twisting its phase around its propagation axis and display doughnut-shaped intensity distributions in the beam's cross-section.

The core advantage of the concept is its simplicity. The metasurfaces are fabricated in a single lithography and etching step on standard silicon substrates, compatible with established semiconductor processing. The bulk substrate remains mechanically robust and dissipates heat effectively.

Moreover, because the mechanism tolerates and even benefits from material absorption, it can be extended into the deep and vacuum UV spectral range and can be applied to a multitude of other material platforms. Furthermore, because many biomolecules have characteristic UV absorption signatures, such compact UV metasurfaces could eventually find applications in integrated sensing.

articles.title: How a metabolite protects the enzyme that consumes it
articles.dek: Metabolites are consumed by enzymes to produce other vital molecules as well as to control metabolite levels. But how do cells avoid consuming too much?
paragraphs: Metabolites are consumed by enzymes to produce other vital molecules as well as to control metabolite levels. But how do cells avoid consuming too much? Researchers from the MPI of Biochemistry, with the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and the de Duve Institute in Brussels, have deciphered such molecular regulation in tryptophan metabolism. The essential amino acid tryptophan binds to a second site on the enzyme TDO2, distinct from where it is consumed. This sequesters a region needed by two effectors, the kinase CK2 and the ubiquitin ligase CUL1–β-TrCP, which act sequentially to signal TDO2 degradation. The findings are now published in Molecular Cell .

The essential amino acid tryptophan is a key building block for proteins and also serves as a precursor for serotonin, melatonin, niacin (vitamin B3) and NAD+. These molecules are vital for the nervous and immune systems and the cell's energy supply. As tryptophan can only be obtained through dietary supply, the body must maintain tryptophan levels within a physiological range.

The enzyme tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO2) carries out the first and rate-limiting step of the kynurenine pathway. While the cell requires the downstream products of TDO2, it must also avoid consuming too much tryptophan.

Researchers have known since the 1950s that TDO2 is stable when there is sufficient tryptophan and is rapidly broken down when tryptophan supply is limiting. It has recently been shown that this feedback mechanism relies on the ubiquitin-proteasome system, the cellular system that marks and degrades unwanted proteins. How tryptophan controls this system has now been elucidated.

Alina Thielen, the first author of the study, explains, "To identify the molecular mechanism underlying TDO2 degradation, we conducted a genome-wide CRISPRi screen. This enabled us to discover the two proteins controlling the degradation process: the kinase CK2 and the E3 ligase CUL1–β-TrCP. To understand their mechanism of action, we performed biochemical reactions with purified proteins in a test tube and used cryo-electron microscopy to examine the structure of TDO2 with and without tryptophan occupying the second binding site."

The kinase and E3 ligase proteins act sequentially on TDO2 to mark it for degradation. When tryptophan becomes scarce, the kinase CK2 attaches phosphate groups to TDO2. This phosphorylation serves as a recognition signal for the E3 ligase CUL1–β-TrCP, which then attaches ubiquitin to TDO2. Ubiquitin-tagged TDO2 is recognized by the proteasome, the cell's waste disposal system.

Thielen explains, "It was already known that tryptophan binds to a second site on TDO2, which is located distal from the catalytic center. Using cryo-electron microscopy, we were able to see how tryptophan organizes a section of the protein near this second binding site to stabilize TDO2. This section folds over the bound tryptophan like a flap, so that the nearby recognition sequence for CK2 and CUL1–β-TrCP is inaccessible.

"If the tryptophan level drops, tryptophan dissociates from the second binding site. As a result, the flap becomes unstructured, making the recognition sequence for CK2 and CUL1–β-TrCP accessible and thereby initiating the process of protein degradation."

Upregulation of TDO2 has been observed in neurological disorders and various types of cancer. In tumors, elevated TDO2 levels can weaken the antitumor immune response. TDO2 is therefore a potential target for new therapeutic agents.

Brenda Schulman explains, "A detailed understanding of TDO2 regulation is important to be able to utilize TDO2 as a therapeutic target. A drug that targets the site where the enzyme consumes tryptophan could also bind to the second binding site and thereby promote unintended TDO2 stabilization. On the other hand, a molecule that occupies the second binding site but keeps the recognition sequence for CK2 and CUL1–β-TrCP accessible could induce the degradation of TDO2."

Schulman summarizes the new findings: "Tryptophan is not only a metabolite and substrate for TDO2—it also acts as a signal that determines how long the TDO2 enzyme remains stable within the cell. Our study reveals a general principle for how a metabolite directly controls the stability of the enzyme that consumes it, thereby linking the cell's metabolism to protein degradation. We are now investigating how cells use this strategy more widely to regulate metabolism according to nutrient supply."

articles.title: New method measures microplastics in the air using an uncrewed aerial system
articles.dek: Microplastics have been found in our bodies and the food we eat—and even in remote environments around the world, including seawater and ice in the Arctic.
paragraphs: Microplastics have been found in our bodies and the food we eat—and even in remote environments around the world, including seawater and ice in the Arctic. Despite their prevalence, little is known about how they move through the atmosphere. New CIRES-led research , which demonstrates a new method for sampling microplastics in the atmosphere using an uncrewed aerial system (UAS), aims to change that. The findings are published in the journal Scientific Reports .

"Atmospheric microplastics are usually sampled from a rooftop, ground-based location or ship," said Radiance Calmer, a former CIRES researcher who is now working at the Norwegian Polar Institute and lead author of the paper. "Our proof-of-concept study shows we can sample atmospheric microplastics using UAS flights for a specific height."

Their results not only indicate microplastics are present 100 meters (328 feet) high in the atmosphere near areas with intense human activity but also confirm the team's UAS sampling method is a feasible approach for measuring microplastics in the atmosphere. They are the first team to successfully use an environmental cyclone sampler on a UAS to collect microplastics.

The work establishes a potential framework for atmospheric microplastics sampling in remote environments, including above the ocean and in the lower atmosphere, where traditional sampling methods are limited and often cost-prohibitive.

"Microplastics can be transported to places people aren't looking for them, making them hard to track," said Gijs de Boer, the Environment & Energy Division director at Brookhaven National Laboratory and a co-author who was a faculty research scientist at CIRES and CU Boulder.

Tracking these tiny particles is important because they are potentially harmful to human health and have unknown impacts on important Earth system processes, such as cloud formation and sea ice melting.
The new project was an engineering and atmospheric science puzzle, bringing together experts from CIRES, CU Boulder and the University of Rhode Island (URI).

First, the team adapted an instrument commonly used in aerosol monitoring—an environmental cyclone sampler—to capture particles from 1 to 10 micrometers in size and attached it to a small UAS. Since the concentration of microplastics in the atmosphere is small, they then had to adapt their sampling method to ensure they captured enough particles.

"The challenge was to sample a large enough volume of air to ensure that some microplastics were present among all the particles," Calmer said. "It was not easy because of the limited UAS flight time, which was around 25 minutes."
In fall 2024, the team deployed their instrument above two sites in Colorado: near a heavily trafficked highway in Erie and residential areas and a landfill in Arvada.

After the UAS flights, the samples were preprocessed at CU Boulder to separate the microplastics from organic particles. The samples then traveled to URI, where researchers counted and identified each particle by plastic type.
Their samples were dominated by clusters of plastic and environmental material called hetero-aggregates, which are often found near highways and areas with high levels of human activity.

articles.title: Future warming events will outdo the extreme heat waves of the recent past, new study finds
articles.dek: The extreme heat waves we have seen over the last few years may only serve as a preview of what is to come as a result of climate change.
paragraphs: The extreme heat waves we have seen over the last few years may only serve as a preview of what is to come as a result of climate change. A new study led by researcher Philipp Aglas-Leitner from Freie Universität Berlin, published in Nature Communications , finds that future heat waves could last longer, impact larger areas, and be much more severe.

In the study "Recent extreme heatwaves are no match for future events," the research team analyzed 22 exceptional heat waves that occurred between 2010 and 2023 in regions such as Europe, Australia, China, India and Pakistan, North Africa and the Middle East, and South America. Nine heat waves from between 2015 and 2023 were investigated in depth. The researchers then compared these events with climate model projections for the period from 2020 to 2100.

Unlike analyses that observe individual temperature records, this new study investigates several heat wave characteristics at the same time, such as duration, cumulative heat, median and maximum event severity, and median and maximum spatial extent of locally heat-affected areas.

Two independent reference data sets from Berkeley Earth and ERA5 were used to analyze the 22 exceptional heat waves. The team used multimodel ensembles from the international model comparison projects CMIP5 and CMIP6 to create climate projections and assessed different scenarios, ranging from substantial emissions reductions through to scenarios with high and very high emissions, as well as a number of different global warming levels.

"The results demonstrate a clear pattern across different climate model ensembles and emission scenarios: A substantial proportion of future heat waves surpass exceptional events in the recent lived experience. They could last longer, impact larger areas, be more severe and produce much higher accumulated temperature anomalies. Recent observed events are outmatched by a substantial margin, particularly toward the end of the 21st century," says Philipp Aglas-Leitner, first author of the study from the Department of Physics and Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Freie Universität Berlin.

The study's projections of severe heat waves are especially striking. The authors state that they will become much more frequent in many regions in the period from 2015 to 2054. The majority of the model ensembles for a lot of the regions investigated are projected to have at least one exceptional heat wave period per year between 2060 and 2099. In Europe, future heat waves could stretch out over several months and impact a significant portion of the continent.

"Our results clearly demonstrate that many of the extreme heat waves that people today have experienced in recent years could be outmatched by those of the future. This has far-reaching implications for human health, infrastructure and ecosystems," Aglas-Leitner explains. "Even ambitious emission reduction goals offer only limited protection. Without substantial emission reductions and consistent adaptation measures, however, a significant part of the 21st century will be defined by heat that goes far beyond our recent experiences."

articles.title: Light-powered method resurrects 'dead-end' compounds for drug discovery
articles.dek: Throughout the drug development process, which can take a decade or more, tens of thousands of chemical compounds are produced that never go on to become medicines.
paragraphs: Throughout the drug development process, which can take a decade or more, tens of thousands of chemical compounds are produced that never go on to become medicines. A Florida State University researcher is part of a team that has discovered a new way to give some of these "dead ends" a second chance at becoming the foundation for tomorrow's blockbuster drugs.

Assistant professor of chemistry and biochemistry Bryan Kudisch and his collaborators have developed a light-powered chemical reaction that can transform a difficult-to-repurpose class of compounds known as sulfonamides into useful building blocks for future drug discoveries. Their research was published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society .

"Kudisch is a molecular spectroscopist who develops and applies laser-based techniques to measure extraordinarily short-time processes, particularly chemically important processes induced by light," said Wei Yang, Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry chair. "His work demonstrates both exceptional technical ability and extraordinary insight into some of the most fundamental and complex processes in chemistry. This publication addressed an important problem closely related to drug discovery, which is a major strategic area of the FSU ASPIRE initiative."

Sulfonamides—which appear in and give rise to the name "sulfa drugs"—are one of the most important molecular substructures in medicinal chemistry. These synthetic medications were some of the first widely used antibiotics almost 90 years ago. Today, they're still used and found in a variety of medicines that treat diseases and symptoms including type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, HIV and melanoma.

Despite their usefulness in many pharmaceuticals, sulfonamides are difficult to repurpose because they are chemically inert. Chemists have developed recipes to interconvert many other functional groups that change the biological properties of a compound, but relatively few options are available to do this with sulfonamides—especially for the sulfur atom that lies at the center of these substructures. Removing this atom or replacing it with a new chemical group could allow researchers to create new versions of existing compounds while preserving their other useful features.

Kudisch and his collaborators addressed this challenge by using a photochemical reaction that converts sulfonamides into anilines, a different class of chemical compounds that serves as the foundation for some cancer-fighting medicines. By transforming part of the molecular structure, otherwise dead-end compounds once again become potential starting points for developing new medicines.

"This outcome was achieved through a chemical 'surgery' that uses light to excise a sulfur atom from a sulfonamide," Kudisch said. "We're optimistic these types of photochemical surgical tools could underpin a range of powerful processes for reshaping molecules that could advance the development of new medicines."
To better understand the molecular reaction during this excision, Kudisch used advanced laser spectroscopic methods to observe the reaction as it happened within a single microsecond.

"We essentially spy on what the light is doing to sulfonamides," Kudisch said. "Our research focuses on what photochemistry secrets are encoded in this transformation. We can track the molecules to understand how they transition into structures that eventually become the desired product or unwanted side product."

Kudisch collaborated with assistant professors of chemistry Eric Nacsa and Elvira Sayfutyarova at Pennsylvania State University as well as pharmaceutical company GSK on the research. Kudisch's group conducted experimental studies to investigate the reaction's mechanism while Sayfutyarova completed computational studies explaining how the reaction occurs. Nacsa's group discovered and optimized the reaction, demonstrated its broad applications and conducted additional mechanistic studies. GSK helped show the potential application of the new reaction in drug discovery.

"Experimental contributions from the Kudisch Lab at FSU combined with computational work by the Sayfutyarova group at Penn State were critical for understanding the reaction's mechanism," Nacsa said. "We anticipate these results and ongoing collaborations with the Kudisch group will provide new fundamental insight into how light can transform molecular structures."

With structure-based drug design becoming more essential for efficient medicine development, this technique can play a key role in contributing to new drug discoveries when applied to different groups of molecules.

articles.title: Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest
articles.dek: Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
paragraphs: Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship.
As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America.

Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru . He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital. In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has drastically cut funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people.

And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero. A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero was assassinated in 1980 after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the U. S. -supported Salvadoran military . His ministry was influenced by liberation theology , a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru.
The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutiérrez , a Peruvian theologian and priest. He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “ A Theology of Liberation .”

Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty to liberate the oppressed . They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins. While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism.

Catholics inspired by liberation theology created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor. In my own research , I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives.

Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about analyzing society and the economy to better understand inequality . In nations like Peru, which possessed rich natural resources , liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers.
During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism.

A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism. Christians for Socialism , for example, argued that liberation meant rejecting capitalism . Some clergy, although only a handful, even picked up arms to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups.

In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – the current pope’s namesake – published “Rerum Novarum ,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution. Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies.

During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics , including some in Chulucanas, Peru , where Leo began his missionary work. Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression.

But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978. For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion. A staunch opponent of communism , he worried about liberation theology’s use of Marxist analysis. So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI.

The Vatican began investigating some liberation theologians for violations of church teachings. In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a year of silence – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy. Several priests were suspended over their work in Sandinista Nicaragua.
John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over Marxism’s influence on his work . Gutiérrez was ultimately not punished.

One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s. The Shining Path , a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru.

Under President Alberto Fujimori, the government escalated existing counterinsurgency operations, often using indiscriminate violence against citizens in the region where the Shining Path emerged. In 2009, Fujimori was convicted of human rights violations .

Leo has never described himself as a liberationist Catholic. However, his experiences as a priest were indelibly shaped by liberation theology , the Peruvian armed conflict and the church debates that roiled much of Latin America during his years there.

Leo, born Robert Prevost, was raised in Chicago. After ordination, his journey as a priest began in Peru, where he landed for missionary work in 1985. The young friar followed in the footsteps of other U. S. Catholic missionaries who had been serving among Peru’s poor and Indigenous, urban and rural, since the 1940s.

Sent to Chulucanas, in Peru’s coastal northwest, Prevost found himself in a region of pastoral experimentation. Since the 1960s, Augustinian missionaries had been working closely with the community to provide literacy education, discussion groups about poverty and inequality, and workshops to train artisans.

These programs were a far cry from the more radical actions of some Catholics who supported liberation theology. Nevertheless, the programs in Chulucanas aimed to empower the Peruvian poor, chipping away at exploitation and low wages on the region’s sugarcane and cotton estates. Like Gutiérrez, many Peruvian Christians believed that the Shining Path drew support because of pervasive poverty and inequality , and that churches could help transform the nation.

But the Catholic Church in Latin America was in the midst of another transformation. John Paul gradually appointed conservative bishops across the continent. Experimental pastoral programs lost support, and institutions that trained priests to put liberation theology into action, such as the Regional Seminary of the Southeast in Mexico, were shuttered or “reoriented.”

Yet even as the hierarchy shifted conservative, work on the ground among Latin America’s poorest continued apace. From coffee cooperatives in Mexico to human rights activists across the continent, many programs survived.

Leo’s 2026 itinerary includes multiple stops that speak to this history and on-the-ground pastoral work. The most symbolic, perhaps, is the Capilla San Óscar Romero, located in Chiclayo, the pope’s former diocese.

articles.title: Could Type 2 Diabetes Be Reversed? 14-Year Study Reveals Remarkable Results
articles.dek: In a long-term trial, weight-loss surgery led to more type 2 diabetes remissions than intensive medical and lifestyle management, while patients’ disease histories offered…
paragraphs: In a long-term trial, weight-loss surgery led to more type 2 diabetes remissions than intensive medical and lifestyle management, while patients’ disease histories offered clues to who might benefit most.

For some people with type 2 diabetes, keeping blood sugar under control without medication is possible. This state, known as remission, raises a question that could shape years of treatment decisions: Which approaches give people the best chance of reaching it, and what makes it more likely to last?

A long-term study found that 58% of participants assigned to weight-loss surgery achieved remission during follow-up, compared with 3% of those assigned to intensive medical and lifestyle management. Participants were followed for a median of 11 years, with some followed for up to 14 years. Those percentages describe how many people reached remission, rather than how many remained in remission throughout that time.

Researchers analyzed data from 262 people with type 2 diabetes, including 166 assigned to metabolic-bariatric surgery, commonly called weight-loss surgery, and 96 assigned to medical and lifestyle management. They defined remission as an A1C below 6. 5% without blood sugar-lowering medication. A1C is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The findings were published in Diabetes Care , a journal of the American Diabetes Association®. They come from the Alliance of Randomized Trials of Medicine vs. Metabolic Surgery in Type 2 Diabetes (ARMMS-T2D), the largest, longest-running trial of metabolic surgery for diabetes. The study’s lead author is Donald Simonson, M. D. , MPH, Sc. D. , of Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston.

Participants who had lived with diabetes for fewer years, did not use insulin, and took fewer types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment were more likely to achieve remission. Greater weight loss during the first year after treatment was also associated with a higher likelihood of remission.

Among people who initially reached remission, diabetes was more likely to return in those who had lived with the disease longer and those who took more types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment. Together, these associations suggest that a patient’s diabetes history and response to treatment may help physicians assess both the likelihood of remission and its potential duration.

The study’s principal investigator, John P. Kirwan, Ph. D. , was named executive director of the University of Oklahoma Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center this summer. He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the University of Oklahoma and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

“For years, one of the most consequential questions in diabetes care has been whether the benefits of metabolic surgery endure,” Kirwan said. “Now we have a durable answer. Over 14 years, 58% of surgical patients achieved remission, compared with just 3% on medication and lifestyle alone. By identifying who is most likely to achieve lasting remission, including shorter diabetes duration, no insulin use, and greater early weight loss, we can offer surgery to the right people earlier, rather than as a last resort.”

Kirwan has led the study since its inception, through his years at the Cleveland Clinic and the Pennington Biomedical Research Center at Louisiana State University. He now brings his expertise in translational and clinical research to the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus.

“Recruiting Dr. Kirwan to lead the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center brings to Oklahoma one of the world’s foremost authorities on long-term treatment for type 2 diabetes,” said Gary Raskob, Ph. D. , Senior Vice President and Provost of the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “Research of this caliber is exactly what this center, and Harold Hamm’s investment in it, was created to advance.”

articles.title: Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stands on the shoulders of Stacey Abrams, Charlotta Bass and countless other Black women who dreamed
articles.dek: There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers.
paragraphs: There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers.
The auction blocks . The cotton fields . The lynching trees . The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves.
And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected Georgia’s first Black woman governor . The first Black woman elected governor of any American state.
Bottoms has traced her ancestry back five generations to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia.
An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil. A descendant elected to govern it.
The same earth. An entirely different claim to power. How many women had to believe in a future they would never live to see?

Bottoms’s victory represents the paradox of Black political advancement amid racial violence and the often-unrecognized labor of women who build futures they may never inhabit. Ultimately, Bottoms’ victory reflects both extraordinary progress and the unfinished work of American democracy.

Between 1979 and 1981, Atlanta was terrorized by the disappearances and murders of Black children and young adults. Mothers pleaded for answers. Families lived in a city where childhood itself had become dangerous.

The murders unfolded just years after Maynard Jackson’s historic 1973 election as Atlanta’s first Black mayor. His victory announced a new era of Black political power. Yet that power could not shield the city’s most vulnerable children. Suspicions of Ku Klux Klan involvement circulated , although the Klan’s responsibility was never established.

Bottoms was born in 1970 . She was 9 when the murders began. She grew up in the same Atlanta where Black parents searched desperately for their missing children. She belonged to the generation whose futures were being stolen. And now she is preparing to lead the entire state.
Those murdered children were not symbols waiting to become useful to history. They were sons and daughters who deserved the ordinary miracle of growing older. They deserved a future.

Bottoms later occupied the mayor’s office that Jackson first opened to Black leadership. Now she is preparing to occupy the governor’s mansion. History has not erased its cruelty. But it has delivered an astonishing answer.
This victory belongs, in no small measure, to democracy advocate, legislator and lawyer Stacey Abrams . Perhaps those who recognize what Abrams made possible have sent her flowers.

Abrams ran for Georgia governor in 2018 and 2022. She lost both races . But through the New Georgia Project and Fair Fight , organizations focused on engaging voters and protecting voting rights, she helped build an electorate that could imagine Georgia differently. She registered voters, challenged barriers to participation , and refused to accept that the South’s political future was fixed.

And now another Black woman has won the office Abrams twice sought, in the third gubernatorial race in a row headed by a Black Democratic woman . There is something biblical about the path Abrams steadfastly cleared. I think of Moses, guiding his people toward the Promised Land but never entering it himself.

Abrams’ journey is not over. Nor should her accomplishments be measured by another woman’s victory. But I believe there is sacred work in preparing a future you may never personally enjoy. Some people plant trees. Some people sit in their shade. Stacey Abrams planted. Bottoms is standing beneath the branches.
And as a scholar of Black media history , I can reach even further back, to another woman who understood the audacity of claiming political power: Charlotta Bass .
In 1952, Bass became the first Black woman nominated for vice president of the United States, running on the Progressive Party ticket.
Before the Voting Rights Act in 1965, before the March on Washington in 1963, before Jackson was elected mayor in 1973 and before Abrams or Bottoms drew their first breaths, there was Bass.

A Black newspaper publisher who confronted segregation, police brutality and white supremacist violence in her four-decade ownership of The California Eagle , Bass understood that political power was about more than winning office. It was about who had the right to imagine themselves in one.

Bass ran when a Black woman entering the White House seemed almost unimaginable. Almost. But not to her. I imagine she would have loved this election. And I suspect she would have had pointed questions for Gov. -elect Bottoms.
What will you do for the poor? The disenfranchised? How will you protect the vote that brought you here?

History-making is not the same as justice-making, and representation matters. The true measure of Bottoms’ victory will be whether Georgians experience the more just state she promised to bring about .

For generations, Black women have been asked to save a democracy that would not save them. We have carried clipboards, protest signs and entire movements on our backs. We have been told to wait. To be patient. To be grateful.

articles.title: The Secret to Saving Shellfish From Acidifying Oceans Could Be Hiding in Crushed Shells
articles.dek: Crushed shells helped young clams grow larger shells in laboratory tests, showing how a long-standing Indigenous coastal practice can offer local protection against ocean…
paragraphs: Crushed shells helped young clams grow larger shells in laboratory tests, showing how a long-standing Indigenous coastal practice can offer local protection against ocean acidification.

For a young clam, the surrounding water can threaten the shell it is trying to grow. When seawater absorbs excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it becomes more acidic, making shell growth more difficult and energetically costly for animals such as clams, oysters, and mussels. Acidic seawater can even dissolve shells. Larvae and juveniles are thought to be especially vulnerable to this process, known as ocean acidification.

Indigenous communities have long added crushed shells to coastal sands to help keep these ecosystems healthy. Research from the University of California, Davis now helps explain how this material, called shell hash, can protect young clams from some of acidification’s effects. Published in Biogeosciences , the study connects the chemistry of water between sand grains with changes in clam growth and gene activity.

At the UC Davis Bodega Marine Laboratory, researchers raised baby Pacific littleneck clams in four conditions. Two groups burrowed in sediment beneath either non-acidified or acidified seawater. The other two experienced the same seawater conditions, but their sediment contained shell hash. During the 90-day experiment, the team tracked shell growth and sampled the seawater three times a week, monitoring acidity, salinity, temperature, and dissolved oxygen.

“We found that, on average, clams grew larger shells when shell hash was present in their treatment,” said study first author Hannah Kempf, an environmental scientist at the California State Water Board who graduated from UC Davis with a Ph. D. in earth and planetary sciences in 2024. “Interestingly, we also found that, on a genetic level, the ‘acidification’ signal was dramatically minimized when shell hash was present.”

The crushed shells altered the chemistry of the water filling the tiny spaces between sand particles, reducing its overall acidity and creating better conditions for shell growth. That finding places the protection at a very local scale, in the water surrounding the burrowing clams.

“Adding crushed shells removed the negative genetic changes that occur when young clams are raised in acidified water,” said study corresponding author David Gold, an associate professor of earth and planetary sciences at UC Davis.

To examine gene activity, the researchers collected samples of the clams’ mantle tissue, which produces their shells, after 90 days and used them for follow-up gene sequencing. The analysis revealed gene expression profiles, or patterns of activity across genes. In clams raised in acidified seawater with shell hash, those profiles were largely indistinguishable from those of clams raised in non-acidified water.
“This was the first time the question was studied from a genetic perspective,” Gold said.

Traditional ecological knowledge provides significant evidence that shell hash benefits shell-making animals, said study co-author Tsim Schneider, an associate professor of anthropology at UC Santa Cruz. In the Pacific Northwest, some Indigenous communities build large-scale structures that expand intertidal spaces, the areas of shore between high and low tide. These structures promote habitat for invertebrates and other marine organisms.

“For me, one of the interesting aspects of this research is the potential to engage more fully with tribes on designing projects that promote their long-standing expertise and Indigenous science,” said Schneider, who is also affiliated with the National Science Foundation’s Center for Braiding Indigenous Knowledges and Science. “If there’s a history of adding shell hash to clam beds in California, for example, western science might be able to better support communities interested in reawakening dormant cultural knowledge and coastal stewardship practices.”
The research was supported by a California Sea Grant and the Russell J. and Dorothy S. Bilinski Fellowship.

articles.title: Earthquake Faults Can Suddenly Become Almost As Fluid as Water, Study Finds
articles.dek: Scientists have uncovered evidence of an unexpected process that may allow earthquake faults to slip enormous distances.
paragraphs: Scientists have uncovered evidence of an unexpected process that may allow earthquake faults to slip enormous distances.

Rocks along Japan’s Boso Peninsula have preserved evidence of an extraordinary process that may occur during powerful earthquakes. Researchers discovered ancient fault structures suggesting that clay trapped between moving rock surfaces became nearly as fluid as water, potentially allowing the fault to slip enormous distances with little resistance.

The findings, from a research team led by Professor Tetsuro Hirono of Osaka Metropolitan University, could help explain how some earthquakes produce the massive seafloor movements capable of triggering devastating tsunamis.

The researchers examined exposed rocks that formed in an ancient seafloor environment approximately 15 million years ago. Within an old earthquake fault, they identified unusual wavy and curved layers, along with swirling structures resembling vortices formed by moving fluids.

The team described these formations as “turbulent-flow-like.” Using fluid dynamics to analyze their shapes, the scientists found evidence that a process called thermal pressurization had caused clay within the fault to become fluidized.

Thermal pressurization occurs when rapid movement along a fault generates intense frictional heat. As water trapped in microscopic spaces within the rock heats up, pressure increases, reducing the frictional resistance that normally keeps the fault surfaces locked together. This weakening can allow much greater movement during an earthquake.

“Our analysis suggests that the viscosity approached that of water,” Professor Hirono explained. “This would have been a dramatic reduction. The fluidized state would have acted as a form of dynamic lubrication, causing the fault to weaken dramatically. The resulting large-scale slip would have produced a large displacement on the fault near the seafloor, potentially causing a tsunami.”

The mechanism could help explain the extreme seafloor displacement associated with some major earthquakes. In 2011, a magnitude 9. 1 earthquake struck eastern Japan, with shaking and fault rupture lasting nearly six minutes. The earthquake shifted the ocean floor enough to generate a devastating tsunami. Although the ancient rocks do not establish whether the same weakening process occurred in 2011, they provide physical evidence of how faults may undergo dramatic changes during seismic events.

The researchers hope to apply their analytical methods to modern faults, using changes in the viscosity of fault materials to better estimate how far those faults might slip during an earthquake. More accurate assessments of fault movement could improve estimates of potential seafloor displacement and associated tsunami hazards.

“Understanding the change in viscosity in fault-slips may allow us to more accurately recognize the magnitude of fault slips, which would support tsunami mitigation efforts,” Professor Hirono concluded.

articles.title: Young people turned out in near-record numbers for the 2026 midterms, with the economy top of their minds
articles.dek: The economy was the top issue for voters in the November 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats win decisive majorities in both houses of Congress.
paragraphs: The economy was the top issue for voters in the November 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats win decisive majorities in both houses of Congress.

And for young voters, whether in college or not, the economy and jobs, as well as healthcare, were their top concerns, our research at CIRCLE , a nonpartisan, research organization focused on youth civic engagement at Tufts University, shows.

Overall, 27% of young people – meaning people ages 18 to 29 – went to the polls during the midterms, our Nov. 5 analysis shows. This marks the second-highest midterm youth voter turnout in the past 30 years, behind only the 2018 election cycle.

As a scholar at CIRCLE who studies young people and their voting behavior, I think it’s helpful to understand some of the factors that motivated so many young people to vote – and to cast their lot with the Democrats.
Among youth, being enrolled as a college student or not did not make a big difference in who they voted for during these midterms.

But there are some voting trend differences based on young people’s educational attainment, especially in the gap between young people with an education level of high school or less, and those with at least some college experience and more. Those with only a high school degree or less voted Democratic by a 24-point margin, compared with a 42-point margin among those with at least some college education.

College students who are young men also voted Democrat by a 24-point margin . Female college students, meanwhile, voted Democrat at a 45-point margin. A similar gender gap appears among young voters who aren’t in college.
Overall, this gender gap has persisted at least since 2024, as young women then were also voting more Democratic than men were.

About 66% of young people ages 18-29 voted for a Democratic candidate for the U. S. House of Representatives, compared with 31% for a Republican candidate, our data shows. This marks the highest percentage of support for Democratic candidates among all age groups.
Within this group, 70% of young women voted for a Democratic U. S. House candidate in the midterms, as opposed to 59% of young men.
Partisan trends among young voters have fluctuated over the past few decades – in 2000, for example, 49% of young people voted Democratic, while 48% voted Republican.

In 2026, Asian American and Pacific Islander, Black and Latino young people gave Democrat candidates the strongest support, at 81%, 79% and 71%, respectively. By comparison, 61% of white young people voted for Democratic House candidates, with 36% voting Republican.
Across race, education, income and geographic location, young people overwhelmingly indicated that the economy and jobs was their top issue in this election.
Healthcare and the Iran war also showed up as areas of importance for young voters. All three of these issues are connected to young people’s concerns about the cost of living.
We found that voting preferences did vary according to how young people viewed their own financial circumstances, a pattern that held among college students.
Low-income students were more likely than their affluent peers to vote for Democrats .
The issues that matter most to young people have shifted considerably over the past several years.
In 2020, we were seeing different groups of young people prioritize social issues like racism , climate change and gun control.
In 2022, we began to see young people prioritize the economy – their concern about inflation was the second-most important issue to them after abortion.

Now, after the economy , healthcare was ranked second for young voters. The third-most important issue was the war in Iran. This is striking, because in the past, we’ve polled young voters about foreign policy issues like the war between Israel and Palestinians and the war between Russia and Ukraine. Young people have never really ranked these other foreign policy issues as a top area of concern.

Youth voter turnout generally tends to be much weaker in midterm elections than in presidential elections. In 2018, there was 28% turnout for young people – a midterm turnout that was considerably higher than 2014, when only 13% of young people turned out to vote.

Campaigns seem to recognize that young voters tend to be less politically engaged. For example, our research shows that during the 2024 presidential election cycle, more than 1 in 3 young people were never contacted about the election. Among those without college experience, 48% were never contacted.
Our research still shows that college students face logistical barriers to voting.

Young people are frequent movers, which means they might need to reregister whenever they change addresses. The fact that college students may be living on campus while they’re registered to vote from their parents’ address can also create complications.

articles.title: What C.S. Lewis said about Narnia’s most famous character: the Jesus-like lion Aslan
articles.dek: As Netflix teases glimpses of Greta Gerwig’s newest project , an adaptation of C. S. Lewis’ novel “The Magician’s Nephew,” many Narnia fans are worried .
paragraphs: As Netflix teases glimpses of Greta Gerwig’s newest project , an adaptation of C. S. Lewis’ novel “The Magician’s Nephew,” many Narnia fans are worried . In particular, there’s been online chatter about the new film’s depiction of the great lion Aslan: Will he really look like David Bowie , with the voice of Meryl Streep ?

For many readers, Aslan is not just a literary character, nor an ordinary hero: He is a representation of Jesus . Aslan sings the entire world of Narnia into existence and performs Christ-like acts throughout Lewis’ “ Chronicles of Narnia ,” which have sold over 120 million copies worldwide since the series’ publication in the 1950s.

As a scholar of medieval history and literature, I’ve taught and written about Lewis and “Lord of the Rings” author J. R. R. Tolkien , who were close friends and colleagues for more than 30 years. Lewis himself was a medievalist at Oxford , and both of their popular literary series are steeped in their knowledge of medieval languages, literature, mythology and theology.
Both authors acknowledged the ethical and religious themes of their fiction . Yet Lewis rejected the idea that “The Chronicles” were simply an allegory.

“ The Magician’s Nephew ,” published in 1955, was actually the last book in the series to be completed. Yet it serves as a prequel, narrating the creation of Narnia and the first appearance of its legitimate ruler, Aslan – the Turkish word for “lion.”

Later in the series, Aslan sacrifices himself to save a young British boy, Edmund Pevensie, from the White Witch, Jadis. Aslan is resurrected through his knowledge of “deeper magic,” and royal power passes to the four Pevensie children.

Christian readers have long seen the series as an imaginative retelling of events from the Gospels, intended for children but offering much to adult readers as well. Critics like Philip Pullman , who wrote the 1990s fantasy trilogy “His Dark Materials,” have denounced “The Chronicles” as religious “propaganda .”

Adding to the book’s religious appeal was Lewis’ own very public faith. An atheist since his youth, he returned to worshipping in the Church of England after a famous late-night conversation with Tolkien in September 1931.

The two English professors had bonded over their interest in Norse myths, which Lewis called beautiful “lies breathed through silver.” For the devoutly Catholic Tolkien, however, ancient myths pointed to truths, not lies, and ultimately to the Gospels. He and other Christian friends at Oxford helped Lewis come to accept Christianity as the “true myth.”

Almost immediately, Lewis began writing Christian apologetics , intellectual defenses of his faith, as well as fiction infused with Christian symbolism and theology. In 1947, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine – well on his way to becoming arguably the most famous Christian apologist of the 20th century.

His letters and scholarly work indicate that “The Chronicles” were not meant to be allegorical . In other words, Aslan was not simply a stand-in for Jesus, and the series was not an extended metaphor.
Rather, Lewis called the books “supposals:” a way of asking, “What if?”

Aslan gives “an imaginary answer to the question, ‘What might Christ become like if there really were a world like Narnia and He chose to be incarnate and die and rise again in that world as He actually has done in ours?” Lewis wrote in a 1958 letter . “This is not allegory at all.”

Neither Lewis nor Tolkien approved of easy allegorical readings of their fiction. Both professors argued that imaginative literature was not simply the product of the author and their time , a sealed treasure waiting for a biographical key to unlock its meaning.

And both men knew formal allegory quite well. Lewis’ 1936 book “ The Allegory of Love ” established his reputation as a critic of medieval and Renaissance literature. His 1933 novel “ The Pilgrim’s Regress ” was an allegorical exploration of his own conversion, with characters that personified various abstract concepts and ideologies.

Tolkien wrote the allegorical short story “ Leaf by Niggle ” as a way to explore his own doubts about ever finishing “ The Lord of the Rings .” Like his earlier novel “ The Hobbit ,” “The Lord of the Rings” only came to fruition through Lewis’ constant encouragement.

Narnia came to Lewis’ mind in bits and pieces. During World War II, when he took young evacuees from bombed cities into his home, a lion had haunted his dreams. A few other mental pictures came to him – a faun carrying packages, a lamppost in the snow – and he began writing. Aslan “just insisted on behaving in His own way,” Lewis later wrote to one schoolgirl .

“The Chronicles” were not an allegory, he insisted, but symbolic. As he described in “ The Allegory of Love ,” “The symbolist leaves the given [facts] to find that which is more real.” Myth and symbols can, if used correctly, point to philosophical or theological truths more effectively than realistic fiction, making their created worlds feel more real.

For fans of “The Chronicles,” Narnia feels “real” in this sense – an escape to truth, rather than an escape from truth. Adapting these stories to film, however, always runs the risk of moving further away from what Lewis captured so brilliantly in his prose.

In 2018, the author’s estate sold Netflix the rights to adapt the book series to screen, and Gerwig was later tapped to write and direct at least two Narnia films. Douglas Gresham, one of Lewis’ stepsons, has an executive producer credit on “ Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew ,” and has generally been enthusiastic about the project.

Gerwig herself has expressed her “reverence” for Lewis’ work . “It was the book of my childhood,” she said at a press event in 2024. “It was the book series that I loved, and I lived through, and I spent so much time imagining myself inside of Narnia.”

Intense scrutiny of the project should surprise no one. As with her film “Little Women,” Gerwig is adapting a beloved novel . And this time, it is a novel written by a very public atheist-turned-Christian whose works have inspired the faith of countless others. Still, her “Magician’s Nephew” should not be judged by a trailer and a handful of interviews.

Lewis likely never expected that “The Chronicles” would turn into a live-action film, but he did believe in the power of imaginative art – whether ancient, medieval or modern – to move one toward truth. The virtues Faith, Hope, Charity and Prudence are frequently depicted in the medieval and Renaissance literature that Lewis loved and taught. Fans and filmmaker alike might benefit from remembering these virtues as well.

articles.title: I’m an athletic trainer – here’s how to know when kids sports are too intense
articles.dek: At a recent T-ball game, I was talking with another father who mentioned that his son had never played before.
paragraphs: At a recent T-ball game, I was talking with another father who mentioned that his son had never played before. As we watched our children falling over trying to scoop up a ground ball, we laughed about how they were still figuring everything out. There was something refreshing about seeing kids learn a game without worrying about how well they were playing.

That moment stayed with me. I’ve spent years as an athletic trainer in collegiate and professional sports, helping athletes stay healthy, handle the demands of competition and perform at their best. Today, I’m a clinical associate professor of kinesiology and chief health and performance adviser for an NCAA Division I athletics program. Given my work, you might expect me to take an active role in developing my own children’s athletic abilities, especially in a youth sports culture where early specialization and greater commitment are often seen as advantages.

And I understand the appeal. Like any parent, I want my children to have opportunities, and it’s easy to wonder whether another practice or lesson might help them get ahead. But with twins who are nearly 6, I’m more interested in whether they enjoy sports than how good they become at them.

As they get older, particularly if they want to pursue sports seriously, my role as a parent will change. Right now, I can step back and let them explore. But as training and competition become more demanding, I’ll want to become more involved in understanding and questioning those demands. Research on training, recovery and athletic development can help parents navigate what’s appropriate as their children’s sports experiences intensify.

When I’m watching my children play, I’d rather be their dad than their performance coach. When they ask to practice hitting or throwing, I’m happy to help. They usually decide when we’re done. Twenty minutes? Great. Five minutes? That’s fine too.
Practice matters, but giving children some control over when and how they practice can help keep it from becoming another obligation.

Research involving more than 9,000 young athletes found that children tend to be more motivated to participate in sports when parents support their ability to make decisions about their participation .

As children get older, their goals may change. Some will want to compete at higher levels or focus on a particular sport. Those ambitions deserve support, but giving children a voice doesn’t mean parents should step away from important decisions. As commitments grow, parents may need to ask more questions about training schedules, recovery time and the expectations placed on their children.

I’ve heard parents describe traveling hours for youth sports tournaments, only to discover that many of the teams competing came from the same communities they had traveled from. One parent recalled driving to Houston for a tournament where six of the eight teams were from the Dallas-Fort Worth area.

I understand how families end up in these situations. An extra practice, private lessons or joining a more competitive team can each seem reasonable. Over time, those commitments become expectations, and saying no isn’t always easy when your child is part of a team.

But more training doesn’t automatically produce better athletes. My experience in sports medicine and performance has taught me that improvement depends on how athletes respond to training, not simply how much they do. Training places demands on the body , and athletes need time to adapt.

The American Academy of Pediatrics cautions that excessive training and early specialization are associated with increased overuse injury risk and may contribute to burnout. Risk depends on training volume, recovery and individual development, particularly during adolescence.

As training demands increase, parents should pay attention to how their children are responding, not just whether they’re experiencing pain. Persistent fatigue, declining performance, changes in sleep or a loss of enthusiasm may suggest that recovery isn’t keeping pace with training. Even an athlete who loves their sport can reach a point where the demands become too much. These are reasons for a parent to discuss the workload with their child and coaches, while persistent or worsening pain warrants medical evaluation.

Athletic development also benefits from variety. Running, climbing, jumping and exploring different activities can help develop coordination and a range of movement skills . The International Olympic Committee recommends varied physical activity and developmentally appropriate training, including for children who may eventually specialize.

Just as important is whether young athletes want to keep playing. Children who enjoy sports are more likely to want to continue participating , research shows. When young soccer players were asked what made sports fun , they identified working hard, improving and spending time with teammates. Even the best training program won’t accomplish much if an athlete no longer wants to participate.

In collegiate and professional sports, reviewing performance is routine. After competition, staff identify what worked, what didn’t and what needs attention. But children don’t need a performance review every time they climb into the car.

I let my children start conversations about their games. If they want to talk about a missed ball, something funny or something that upset them, I’ll listen. If they want to talk about something else, that’s fine too.

Researchers who recorded parent-child car rides around sporting events found that much of the time passed in silence and sports came up relatively infrequently . They also observed occasions when parents interrupted or provided feedback before children could respond. The findings don’t establish one right way to handle the drive home, but they offer parents a reason to consider whether their children want feedback in the first place.

No parent knows whether their child will become a competitive athlete, play recreationally or eventually find interests outside organized sports. I’m comfortable leaving that future open for my children. As a father, I’m far more interested in whether my kids will want to play again next week than how well they played today.
