articles.title: What the measles vaccine’s ‘97% effective’ rating means for Pittsburgh parents
articles.dek: Pennsylvania is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades, with more than 1,400 confirmed cases and six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026,…
paragraphs: Pennsylvania is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades, with more than 1,400 confirmed cases and six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, according to statistics compiled by the state.

Each new case brings a new warning of a measles exposure in that community. Exposures have occurred at hospitals and doctors’ offices , grocery stores and restaurants , and K-12 schools and universities .

Exposure alerts come with the same instructions: Check your MMR vaccine status, and watch for symptoms for the next three weeks. People are told that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles. The underlying message is that if you’re vaccinated, you’re protected.
The MMR vaccine is highly effective at preventing disease, but it isn’t a guarantee. People may hear that 97% figure and wonder about the other 3% .

Parents ask me: Should I be worried? How do I know if my kid has measles? Do I need an MMR booster? Most recently, my teenage daughter texted me to ask about her MMR vaccine status. She was worried about what would happen if she were exposed.

These are questions I can answer as both a mother and an epidemiologist in northwestern Pennsylvania . I became both at once. My daughter was born at the start of my doctoral program, and I read epidemiology textbooks aloud to her while studying for my comprehensive exams. I defended my dissertation on my son’s due date. I’m a better mother because I’m an epidemiologist, and a better epidemiologist because I’m a mom.
The advice in each public measles exposure alert matches the guidance doctors follow when a patient may have been exposed.

Everyone is asked to watch for symptoms , whether or not they’re vaccinated. The number of unvaccinated people across Pennsylvania is growing . As a result, many communities , including Allegheny County, no longer have herd immunity.
Four of the over 1,400 confirmed measles cases in Pennsylvania were people who had been vaccinated . These cases are known as breakthrough infections .

The term “herd immunity” wasn’t coined until 1918 . That year, a veterinarian wrote about an outbreak of “contagious abortion” in sheep and cattle, a literal herd. Today, herd immunity means that the risk of disease for susceptible people, those without immunity, drops when they are surrounded by people who are immune.

In other words, if the people around you are immune, you’re unlikely to get sick even if you’re susceptible. For measles, that protection depends on about 95% of people being immune. In a school or community where fewer than 95% of people are vaccinated, measles can spread more easily.
In Allegheny County, 93. 8% of children are fully vaccinated against measles . Some neighborhoods are above 97% uptake, while others are below the necessary 95% needed for herd immunity .

Measles exposures are announced publicly by the Department of Health and local healthcare providers . During a measles outbreak, public health departments may get in touch with close contacts to alert them to an exposure.

Public exposure alerts, like the one made in October after there was a measles exposure at a Target near Pittsburgh , are also used. Public alerts are for settings where exposed people can’t be identified and contacted individually. Measles is so contagious that a single case can infect up to 18 susceptible people .
Measles spreads through the air and through respiratory droplets, like those released when someone sneezes. The virus can also survive outside the body , lingering in the air and on surfaces.

Imagine I have measles and walk into my local grocery store. I’m contagious from about four days before the rash appears until four days after. Every time I breathe out, I release virus particles into the air, and those particles can stay infectious for up to two hours. If I sneeze in the produce section, the virus can survive on surfaces for up to two hours.

However, if you’ve had measles or were vaccinated with two doses of the MMR vaccine, you are protected. Two doses provides 97% lifetime protection against measles . This means that even without herd immunity, fewer than 3% of individuals with immunity are likely to contract measles. Adults who have had measles, or who have documentation of the recommended doses of the MMR vaccine, don’t need a booster .

People who were vaccinated between 1963 and 1967, or who aren’t sure which vaccine they received, should talk to their primary care provider about whether they need another dose. This is because the measles vaccine used between those years was not as effective as the MMR vaccine that is currently given .

Today, children typically get their first dose of the MMR vaccine at 12 to 15 months old and a second dose at 4 to 6 years old . Because the vaccine is given in early childhood, people born in the early to mid-1960s are the most likely to have received the older vaccine. People born before 1957 are generally considered immune , because measles was so widespread then that almost everyone caught it as a child.

Symptoms of measles include a high fever that can reach 105 degrees Fahrenheit (40. 6 degrees Celsius), a cough, a runny nose and conjunctivitis, also known as pin keye. These symptoms overlap with those of other respiratory viruses, such as flu and COVID-19.

Most people with measles develop a red, blotchy rash. It starts on the face and spreads down the body, like paint poured from a bucket . People who are immunocompromised or were previously vaccinated, even with one dose of the MMR vaccine, may not develop the rash. Between 25% and 40% of immunocompromised people with measles never get the rash .
A telltale sign of measles is Koplik spots , tiny white spots inside the mouth that can show up a day or two before the rash.

Measles can have serious consequences. About 1 in 20 people with measles develop pneumonia, and up to 3 in 1,000 cases end in death. Children younger than 5 and adults older than 20 are most likely to experience these severe complications.

Without herd immunity in many communities, measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths in Pennsylvania are likely to keep rising. The state Department of Health reports community spread of measles in 14 of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties .

articles.title: Flesh-eating screwworm is spreading in the US, threatening livestock and wildlife – hunters can be the first line of defense
articles.dek: For the first time in over 50 years, an infestation of the flesh-eating fly known as the New World screwworm ( Cochliomyia hominivorax ) is spreading on the U.
paragraphs: For the first time in over 50 years, an infestation of the flesh-eating fly known as the New World screwworm ( Cochliomyia hominivorax ) is spreading on the U. S. mainland, and it is putting livestock and other animals at risk.
The New World screwworm doesn’t just attack cattle. All warm-blooded animals are susceptible, including deer and elk, as well as small game and waterfowl.
That means hunters headed to the field this fall may be the most important line of defense for spotting this destructive parasite and keeping it from spreading further.

As co-directors of the Mississippi State University deer lab , we believe the country’s millions of hunters can serve as a powerful early warning system by keeping a close eye on the state of wildlife they see. Wildlife agencies are already asking them to be vigilant and report any signs of screwworm infestations .

Unlike other blowflies , New World screwworm larvae feed on living tissue rather than dead tissue. They lay eggs in open wounds or mucosal openings, such as the eyes and nose of livestock, deer or elk.

Wounds as small as tick bites or scratches, as well as natural openings such as the umbilical stump on newborns or on deer’s pedicles , where their antlers grow and are shed, can attract these parasites.
Once the eggs hatch, the maggots burrow into the animal’s flesh and feed, enlarging the wound and attracting more flies. Over time, this leads to infection and death.
All warm-blooded animals are susceptible to the New World screwworm, but America has seen firsthand the harm they can cause to livestock.
In the 1950s, livestock producers in the U. S. Southwest lost up to US$100 million annually to New World screwworm infections, equivalent to over $1 billion today.

The nation was eventually able to eradicate the New World screwworm from the mainland in 1966 using a combination of treating infected animals and raising hundreds of millions of sterilized male flies and releasing them in infested areas.

The New World screwworm has a life cycle of only about 21 days, and each female mates only once. Because of that, inundating areas with sterile male flies for a few months, which equates to a few generations of flies, can eradicate a screwworm population.

Over time, sterile flies were used to push the New World screwworm further south, where they had been contained behind the Darién Gap , Panama’s narrow border region with Colombia. Sterile flies kept the parasite south of Panama for years, but the movement of cattle and wildlife likely brought it north again . Since 2022, the parasites have been reproducing and moving farther northward . There have been hundreds of detections in Mexico and now in the U. S.

Wildlife have received far less attention than livestock during screwworm infestations, with one exception: In July 2016, the New World screwworm was detected in the Florida Keys in an endangered deer population : the Florida Key deer ( Odocoileus virginianus clavium ).

At the time, the Florida Key deer population was estimated at only about 800 to 1,000 individuals . Because they were endangered and isolated, primarily on the islands of Big Pine Key and No Name Key , they were monitored more closely than most wildlife.

U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists established quarantine zones. They inspected more than 16,900 animals – dogs, cats, a pig and a raccoon were also found with larvae – and they released 150 million sterile flies across the area. The islands lost 9% to 20% of the total Key Deer population , but the New World screwworm was declared eradicated there on March 23, 2017, less than a year after it was discovered.

In June 2026, screwworm was back in the United States. A rancher discovered the first New World screwworm case in a calf near La Pryor, Texas. A few more cases were confirmed in livestock and domestic animals in Texas and New Mexico .

The number of cases had reached 116 detections in animals as of Nov. 5, 2026 , including in two elk shot by hunters in Texas . The U. S. government has started ramping up production of sterile flies to try to keep the parasites from spreading.
Although there have been only a couple of cases reported in wildlife, that isn’t necessarily reassuring.

Wildlife are far more likely to carry the parasite without being detected. Once the screwworm is detected, treatment would also be much more complicated for wildlife than for livestock, because wildlife cannot be treated individually and thus are more dependent on the use of sterile flies to eradicate screwworm.
For this reason, quickly identifying areas with New World screwworm and targeting those areas by releasing sterile flies would be more important than ever.
Fortunately, there is an army of conservationists across the country who spend much of their time afield. These conservationists are also known as hunters.

According to the latest U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation, nearly 11. 5 million hunters pursue big game and spend part of the fall and winter in the field hunting ungulate species such as deer and elk.

White-tailed deer ( Odocoileus virginianus ) hunters alone are expected to harvest about 6 million deer during the 2026-27 season and will observe millions more. Hunters also review tens of millions of wildlife pictures collected each year by game cameras used for scouting.

That level of surveillance can’t be matched. New Mexico’s Department of Agriculture has already called on hunters to report any suspicious larvae, particularly in Grant and Otero counties, where screwworm has been found in livestock. Hunters of all kinds, everywhere, can help.

articles.title: Scientists Reveal How a Mysterious Brain Structure Keeps Memories From Fading
articles.dek: Memories that last only seconds shape everyday thinking, and research in mice is revealing how a small brain structure supports an ability impaired in ADHD and schizophrenia.
paragraphs: Memories that last only seconds shape everyday thinking, and research in mice is revealing how a small brain structure supports an ability impaired in ADHD and schizophrenia.

To understand a sentence, the brain has to keep earlier words in mind as new ones arrive. Working memory makes that possible, holding information for a few seconds so we can compare it with new information, manipulate it, and use it to guide our behavior.

We rely on it to follow conversations, solve problems, and decide what to do next. Yet sensory information fades within moments once a stimulus ends, leaving the brain with the demanding task of maintaining a usable representation of something that is no longer there.

In mice, researchers at UNIGE have found that this ability relies partly on the claustrum, a thin structure deep within the brain between the insular cortex and the striatum. Their findings appear in Nature Communications .

The scientists tested mice on tasks that required them to remember either a smell or a touch. Each animal received an initial stimulus, waited several seconds, and then received a second stimulus. The mouse had to determine whether the two were identical or different. By the time the second stimulus arrived, the first was gone, so success depended on retaining information about it during the wait.

Temporarily reducing the activity of claustrum neurons cut the mice’s working memory performance in half. To control these neurons at precise moments during the task, the researchers used techniques including optogenetics. This method uses specific proteins to make selected neurons sensitive to light, allowing scientists to alter their activity through an optical fiber. The intervention helped establish that the claustrum contributes to working memory rather than simply becoming active while another brain region does the necessary work.

“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” says study co-leader Alan Carleton, Full Professor in the Department of Basic Neurosciences at UNIGE’s Faculty of Medicine. “Moreover, disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself.”

Working memory depends on interactions across a broad network that includes the prefrontal cortex, sensory regions, the parietal cortex, the thalamus, and other structures beneath the cortex. These networks must preserve information while allowing the brain to continue perceiving, thinking, and acting, but how they maintain a representation over time remains largely unknown. The claustrum’s anatomy offers a reason to examine its contribution.
“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” explains Carleton.
Recordings from the mice allowed the researchers to examine how information was represented in claustrum activity during the gap between stimuli.

“Our live recordings of claustrum neuron activity showed that a trace of the initial information persisted throughout the entire waiting period,” says fellow study leader Ivan Rodriguez, Full Professor in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE’s Faculty of Science. “Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time. Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”

“Our discovery could help us better understand cognitive disorders in which working memory is impaired, such as schizophrenia or ADHD,” explains Carleton. “Identifying the brain circuits that allow information to be maintained over time is an important step towards understanding how these functions can be disrupted. We now need to determine how the claustrum communicates with cortical networks, and how this interaction preserves the fidelity of the representations held in working memory.”

articles.title: The Hidden Brain Mechanism That Makes You Love Coffee, Chocolate, Fat, and Sugar
articles.dek: Scientists have uncovered a previously understudied dopamine pathway that may explain how we learn to enjoy flavors we initially dislike.
paragraphs: Scientists have uncovered a previously understudied dopamine pathway that may explain how we learn to enjoy flavors we initially dislike.

A food can become more appealing even when its flavor stays exactly the same. Researchers at UC San Francisco have identified a previously understudied dopamine pathway that helps the brain learn which flavors are worth seeking out based on what happens after nutrients reach the gut.

The study, published November 4 in Nature , reveals how a slow chemical signal connects digestion with learned food preferences. The mechanism could help explain why people develop a taste for initially unpleasant flavors, including the bitterness of coffee.

Dopamine helps the brain learn which experiences are rewarding, but most research has examined rapid signals that appear within seconds of external cues, such as seeing a favorite meal. The newly studied “slow” dopamine system responds to events inside the body. When digestive sensors detect nutrients such as sugar and fat, they initiate signals that can sustain dopamine release in the brain for several minutes.

“We’ve shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens,” said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

Coffee provides a familiar example of how this learning may work. Although its bitterness can be unpleasant initially, repeated experiences can teach the brain to associate the flavor with caffeine’s stimulating effects. Once that association develops, Knight explained, “that coffee starts to taste a lot better.”

To isolate the brain’s response to nutrients from its response to taste, Knight and James Grove, PhD, who was then a graduate student, delivered sugar water or a milkshake-like liquid directly into the stomachs of mice. They simultaneously measured dopamine release throughout the brain.

Nutrients entering the stomach produced a strong, sustained dopamine response in the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA. Although researchers already knew this region received dopamine signals, their role in learning about food was unclear.
“We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role,” Knight said.

The researchers next tested whether the pathway was necessary for learning. When they blocked it, the mice continued eating normally but could no longer learn that a particular unfamiliar flavor was associated with calories. This showed that the pathway was important for forming food preferences rather than simply controlling food consumption.

In a separate experiment, the researchers artificially stimulated dopamine fibers in the BLA after mice sampled a calorie-free flavor. The animals subsequently developed a preference for that flavor, even though it provided no nutritional reward.

Together, the experiments demonstrated that dopamine signaling in this region can teach mice to associate a flavor with the beneficial effects of nutrients. Artificial stimulation could substitute for the signal normally generated when nutrients reach the gut.

Human brain imaging provided additional evidence of a similar response. Yale psychologist Dana Small, PhD, reanalyzed an earlier PET study involving 13 men who consumed either a milkshake or a noncaloric drink. Nutrient consumption was associated with dopamine release concentrated in the left BLA.

In another experiment, Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and colleagues used fMRI scans to study 38 adults after glucose consumption. They detected increased activity in the same brain region, although fMRI measures brain activity rather than dopamine release directly.

articles.title: Taking a Gander at Utah’s Goosenecks
articles.dek: Tens of millions of years ago, the San Juan River in what is now southern Utah shared some characteristics with today’s Mississippi River.
paragraphs: Tens of millions of years ago, the San Juan River in what is now southern Utah shared some characteristics with today’s Mississippi River. In a bygone geologic era, the San Juan flowed across a relatively flat plain that formed in an ancient marine environment. Unencumbered by rugged terrain, the river was free to take a long, meandering path on its gradual journey downslope.

But this part of the San Juan changed when geologic forces pushed the Colorado Plateau upward. Some experts think that within the later stages of this “ still-enigmatic ” history, starting around 20 million years ago, the plateau’s rise elevated the San Juan’s headwaters , which increased the river’s gradient and sped its flow. With that, the water’s erosive power intensified, and the river started carving its winding path deeper and deeper through 300-million-year-old rock.

Today, on its westward path to Lake Powell, the San Juan River flows through an impressive series of entrenched meanders, also known as “goosenecks.” An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed the stark desert topography on October 6, 2026.

In Utah’s Goosenecks State Park , the river runs through a canyon 1,000 feet (300 meters) deep. In places, it nearly loops back on itself, making horseshoe-shaped bends. One section is so curvy that the river travels 5. 5 miles (8. 9 kilometers) between two points that are only 1. 3 miles (2. 1 kilometers) apart as the crow—nay, goose—flies.

While the goosenecks are an unusual geologic wonder to behold by day, the area’s dark skies are a spectacle by night. Goosenecks State Park’s remote, high-desert location and 360-degree views of the sky helped earn it an International Dark Sky Park designation in 2021. According to DarkSky International, features such as the Double Cluster in Perseus and the Messier 24 star cloud in the Sagittarius spiral arm of the Milky Way are visible to the unaided eye from the park. In November 2026 , dark skies offer the chance to view several meteor showers, with the Northern Taurids, Southern Taurids, and Leonids reaching their peaks throughout the month.

Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-188830 was acquired on October 6, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimeters. It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The image was taken by a member of the Expedition 75 crew. The image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the internet.

articles.title: A New Era of Bionic Vision? AI Helps Scientists Unlock the Brain’s Visual Cortex
articles.dek: Researchers have used artificial intelligence to improve how a brain implant stimulates the visual cortex of a blind person, potentially advancing the development of bionic eyes.
paragraphs: Researchers have used artificial intelligence to improve how a brain implant stimulates the visual cortex of a blind person, potentially advancing the development of bionic eyes.

Artificial intelligence could make future bionic eyes more precise and responsive by improving how electrical signals communicate with the brain. In a study published in Neuron , researchers used deep learning to control brain stimulation in a blind man, producing more accurate neural responses with less electrical current.
The findings could advance visual prostheses that bypass damaged eyes and optic nerves, stimulating the visual cortex directly to generate perceptions of light.

Researchers from UC Santa Barbara , ETH Zurich , and Miguel Hernández University (MHU) tested the approach in a 27-year-old man who lost his sight following a traumatic brain injury. At a hospital in Spain, a temporary implant containing 96 electrodes stimulated his visual cortex, producing phosphenes, perceived as flashes or shapes of light.

Led in part by UCSB professor Michael Beyeler, the team trained a deep neural network to predict brain responses to different stimulation patterns. The AI model also incorporated measurements of resting brain activity, allowing it to account for changes in the brain’s condition before each test.

The AI-designed stimulation patterns produced targeted neural responses more accurately and required less electrical current than comparison approaches. Researchers also found that recorded brain activity predicted the participant’s visual perceptions better than the electrical settings alone.

“Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image,” Beyeler said. “But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.”

The implant could both stimulate neurons and record their responses, enabling the AI to learn from actual brain activity. The participant also described perceived flashes, including their brightness, size, shape, and color.

The technology could eventually help people who lose their sight through injuries or neurological and inherited conditions. Beyeler emphasized those “who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision,” adding, “For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.”
Describing the international research effort as “a true collaboration,” Beyeler said the study demonstrated how computational models could influence experiments involving human participants.

“Building a model in the abstract is one thing,” he said. “Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.”
Although the research remains an early proof of concept, it suggests that future visual prostheses may work better by continuously adjusting stimulation to an individual’s neural responses.

“A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe,” Beyeler said. “It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.”

articles.title: Scientists Spent 7 Years Studying Moth Wings and Discovered Something Unexpected
articles.dek: A search to change the patterns on moth wings uncovered something unexpected: wider tails, suggesting that evolution may reshape insects’ defenses by modifying features they…
paragraphs: A search to change the patterns on moth wings uncovered something unexpected: wider tails, suggesting that evolution may reshape insects’ defenses by modifying features they already possess.

A luna moth’s leaf-like wings help it escape the notice of predators that hunt by sight. Other giant silk moths display prominent eyespots that can make them look threatening. A new study suggests that moving between those appearances can require only a small change in the signals that guide wing development.

Over seven years, Andrei Sourakov hand-reared more than 700 luna ( Actias luna ) and polyphemus ( Antheraea polyphemus ) moths from egg to adulthood. Sourakov is the collection coordinator of Lepidoptera at the Florida Museum of Natural History and an affiliate associate professor of entomology at the University of Florida. His findings, recently published in Evolution & Development , reveal how treatments during development can alter both the patterns and shapes of moth wings.

Sourakov treated developing moths with small amounts of heparin and dextran sulfate. Both are sulfated polysaccharides, molecules made of linked sugars with attached sulfate groups. They increase the activity of a group of proteins called Wnt, which help direct development.

He administered tiny quantities of heparin shortly before and after pupation, when caterpillars enter the pupal stage and undergo their final transformation into adults. Wing patterns are determined during this period. For two years, the treatments failed to produce the changes he was seeking, so he continued adjusting the concentration and timing of the doses.

“I kept trying, and eventually, I achieved a single transformation. But it wasn’t of the wing pattern. It was the wing shape. This single specimen was so different that I couldn’t ignore it,” he said.

That specimen was a luna moth whose hindwing tails had grown wider than those of any moth he had previously reared. Scientists think luna moths evolved their long tails to deflect bat attacks away from the main part of their bodies.
“I thought, this is very bizarre. Maybe the genes that are normally responsible for wing patterns are here responsible for wing shape, because that’s seemingly the only thing that was transformed.”
Further adjustments to the timing of heparin treatment eventually produced changes in both wing shape and eyespots, overturning that initial explanation.

In polyphemus moths, the yellow borders around the two lemon-shaped eyespots on the forewings thickened. Brown scales surrounding those markings, which normally matched the rest of the wings, became whiter. On the hindwings, the black borders around the eyespots expanded. Together, these changes made the markings more conspicuous.

Luna moths underwent a similarly striking transformation. Their round hindwing eyespots took on a squinting appearance and developed thick, dark borders resembling mascara, turning subtle markings into a more noticeable display. Both heparin and dextran sulfate also changed the shape of luna moth wings, something not previously achieved experimentally in Lepidoptera, the group that includes all moths and butterflies.

“Some giant silk moths have eyespots that make them appear threatening to would-be predators. Others look like leaves, with translucent eyespots resembling holes to make it more convincing. What’s amazing to me, and what I learned from this study, is how easy it is for these features to go from one state to another. They do this without big inventions by simply expanding or contracting existing elements to the point where eyespots look completely different. All they need is a slight increase in the amount of certain compounds at the right moment,” Sourakov said.

Moth and butterfly eyespots occupy different parts of the wings, a clue that they evolved independently. Sourakov’s original goal was to investigate whether the two groups used the same genes to create these markings or had independently arrived at similar designs.

He tested the responses of several giant silk moth species to sulfated polysaccharides, reasoning that similar responses in different species could indicate homologous eyespots, meaning markings with a shared evolutionary origin. Further experiments would be needed to confirm that relationship.

paragraphs: Students in Florida will hear from NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney as they answer prerecorded STEM questions while aboard the International Space Station .

Media interested in covering the event must RSVP no later than 5 p. m. EST, Monday, Nov. 9, to Christina Upchurch at (904) 547-7517, or at christina. upchurch@stjohns. k12. fl. us .

For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth. articles.title: Hubble Learns Galactic History From Stars
articles.dek: This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image provides a lesson in galactic history.
paragraphs: This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image provides a lesson in galactic history. The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 (M30) after the French astronomer, Charles Messier , who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier’s time. M30 lies about 27,500 light-years away in the constellation Capricornus.

M30 is a globular cluster : a roughly spherical grouping of stars containing anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars. These clusters generally reside on the outskirts of galaxies, orbiting within a vast, diffuse region called the halo like a swarm of moths around a lightbulb. Our Milky Way galaxy has at least 150 globular clusters, the nearest of which is about 6,000 light-years away. These clusters are impressively ancient: astronomers estimate their ages are between 11. 5 to 13. 5 billion years, making certain globular clusters nearly as old as the universe itself.

Globular clusters have long played an important role in helping us learn about our galaxy. More than a century ago, astronomer Harlow Shapley used observations of a particular type of variable star to measure the locations of and distances to dozens of globular clusters within our galaxy. His work showed that the Sun is not in the center of our galaxy, and that the galactic center lies toward the constellation Sagittarius. (His distance measurements were incorrect, however, and he concluded that our galaxy is about twice as large as it really is. )

Today, astronomers continue to learn about our galaxy by observing globular clusters. Because globular clusters are so ancient, they can give us clues about how our galaxy developed long ago. Globular clusters that formed within our galaxy can act as time capsules, preserving the original chemistry of our young galaxy.

However, it’s possible that not all globular clusters that orbit within our galaxy today formed there. Researchers have discovered that M30 and many other globular clusters orbit in the direction opposite from the way our galaxy spins. This may mean that these clusters did not form within our galaxy at all. Instead, our Milky Way galaxy may have captured them in the distant past!

Hubble has observed M30 multiple times. A previously released image of M30 featured data from Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and was part of an observing program (# 10775 ; PI: Sarajedini) that surveyed dozens of Milky Way globular clusters in red and near-infrared light, revealing stars down to just 20% of the mass of the Sun. A more recent program (# 13297 ; PI: Piotto) returned to M30 and other globular clusters in our galaxy, this time observing the clusters with Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 and using three filters that captured bluer light.

This program collected data that was critical for studying exotic objects like “ blue straggler ” stars as well as for investigating the multiple populations of stars that can inhabit a single globular cluster.

More recently, Hubble’s ACS viewed many of these globular clusters again. Those observations were part of a program (# 16298 , PI: Libralato) that looked at how different populations of stars in globular clusters moved over the 15 years since Hubble first observed them — a feat made possible by Hubble’s longevity and ability to discern fantastically small details in distant objects.

The image above was created with data from all three observing programs and includes the wide range of wavelengths Hubble can see — ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light. Each wavelength helps us better understand how these groups of stars formed and evolved.
Claire Andreoli NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center , Greenbelt, MD claire. andreoli@nasa. gov

These jewels of the night sky offer us a glimpse at the lifecycle of stars.

These clusters generally reside on the outskirts of galaxies, orbiting within a vast, diffuse region called the halo like a swarm of moths around a lightbulb. Our Milky Way galaxy has at least 150 globular clusters, the nearest of which is about 6,000 light-years away. These clusters are impressively ancient: astronomers estimate their ages are between 11. 5 to 13. 5 billion years, making certain globular clusters nearly as old as the universe itself.

Globular clusters have long played an important role in helping us learn about our galaxy. More than a century ago, astronomer Harlow Shapley used observations of a particular type of variable star to measure the locations of and distances to dozens of globular clusters within our galaxy. His work showed that the Sun is not in the center of our galaxy, and that the galactic center lies toward the constellation Sagittarius. (His distance measurements were incorrect, however, and he concluded that our galaxy is about twice as large as it really is. )

Today, astronomers continue to learn about our galaxy by observing globular clusters. Because globular clusters are so ancient, they can give us clues about how our galaxy developed long ago. Globular clusters that formed within our galaxy can act as time capsules, preserving the original chemistry of our young galaxy.

However, it’s possible that not all globular clusters that orbit within our galaxy today formed there. Researchers have discovered that M30 and many other globular clusters orbit in the direction opposite from the way our galaxy spins. This may mean that these clusters did not form within our galaxy at all. Instead, our Milky Way galaxy may have captured them in the distant past!

Hubble has observed M30 multiple times. A previously released image of M30 featured data from Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and was part of an observing program (# 10775 ; PI: Sarajedini) that surveyed dozens of Milky Way globular clusters in red and near-infrared light, revealing stars down to just 20% of the mass of the Sun. A more recent program (# 13297 ; PI: Piotto) returned to M30 and other globular clusters in our galaxy, this time observing the clusters with Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 and using three filters that captured bluer light.

This program collected data that was critical for studying exotic objects like “ blue straggler ” stars as well as for investigating the multiple populations of stars that can inhabit a single globular cluster.

More recently, Hubble’s ACS viewed many of these globular clusters again. Those observations were part of a program (# 16298 , PI: Libralato) that looked at how different populations of stars in globular clusters moved over the 15 years since Hubble first observed them — a feat made possible by Hubble’s longevity and ability to discern fantastically small details in distant objects.

The image above was created with data from all three observing programs and includes the wide range of wavelengths Hubble can see — ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light. Each wavelength helps us better understand how these groups of stars formed and evolved.

articles.title: Cyprus: Island of Snakes, Cats, and Ophiolites
articles.dek: The island of Cyprus began to form some 90 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous , with molten rock pouring from the seafloor, solidifying, and building new oceanic…
paragraphs: The island of Cyprus began to form some 90 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous , with molten rock pouring from the seafloor, solidifying, and building new oceanic crust . Over time, portions of this oceanic rock were wrenched upward by tectonic forces , eventually emerging as a rugged island made of ophiolite , a type of rock with a mottled green appearance said to look like the skin of a snake. Remnants of that ancient island are still visible in the dark rocks of the Troodos Mountains .

During the Miocene , considerably younger layers of chalk, limestone, marl, and other marine sedimentary rocks accumulated around the island, providing material that developed into a second, smaller island to the south during a later period of geologic uplift . Over time, sediment poured from rivers into the channel separating the two islands and combined with marine sediments to create deltas and eventually two land bridges, or tombolos . The joined landmass comprises the Akrotiri Peninsula , now the southernmost tip of Cyprus.

The sandy edges of the peninsula were visible when Landsat 8 captured these images on October 10, 2026. Akrotiri Salt Lake , a coastal lagoon that was once an arm of the Mediterranean Sea, lies between the two tombolos. The more westerly feature, the Kouris River tombolo, formed first, developing about 50,000 years ago from river-deposited gravels and sands. The eastern tombolo extended southward from Cyprus, cutting off the Mediterranean Sea only within the past 2,000 years, according to geologists .

The lake’s water levels now vary markedly with the seasons, typically filling in the late autumn and winter and drying out in the summer. The influx of winter water has historically attracted sizable overwintering flamingo populations, averaging about 4,000 birds. However, the wintering flamingo population has declined in recent years, plummeting to 30 birds in 2025, according to news reports . Flamingos have long flocked to the lake to feed on fairy shrimp , which are rich in colorful substances called carotenoids that give the birds their famously pink hue .

Snakes are another of the island’s more notorious animal inhabitants. In antiquity, Cyprus was known as Ophiousa , or “ land of snakes ,” likely due to its robust population of blunt-nosed vipers . According to legend, the island’s snake communities grew to be so problematic during a drought in the fourth century that the Roman Empress Helena , mother of Constantine the Great, called for shiploads of cats to be sent from Egypt to control the venomous reptiles.

The first feline imports were released in a particularly snake-infested area on the southeastern part of the Akrotiri Peninsula, an area that came to be known as Cape Gata (Cape Cat in Greek). The cape today is still home to the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats , a place where legend says that monks encouraged newly arrived Egyptian cats to hunt snakes. Today, Cyprus has as many cats as people, with more than one million of the feline predators stalking the island. The handful of nuns who now live in the monastery still care for hundreds of cats, according to the St. Nicholas Center .

articles.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
articles.dek: On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP. Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
paragraphs: On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP. Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies.

The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities.

“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next. We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics. This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.”

The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach . 75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions.

“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” said Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”

The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America’s leadership in aviation. From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today’s X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight.
With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation.
